St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant Unit 1 manually shut down after 3 control rods drop into reactor core
The reactor was manually tripped Wednesday morning while operating at 100% power. The NRC classified the event as a non-emergency, and the plant says all systems responded normally.
Prev
Next
Florida Power and Light
By:
Emma Romano
Posted
and last updated
Unit 1 at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant was manually shut down Wednesday morning after 3 control rods dropped into the reactor core, according to a notification filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).
The manual reactor trip occurred at 9:47 a.m. EDT on Aug. 13, 2026, while Unit 1 was operating at 100% power. The NRC classified the event as a non-emergency.
"At 0947 EDT on August 13, 2026, with Unit 1 in Mode 1 at 100 percent power, the reactor was manually tripped due to 3 control rods dropping into the core. The trip was uncomplicated with all systems responding normally post-trip. Operations stabilized the plant in Mode 3. Decay heat is being removed by discharging steam to the main condenser using the turbine bypass valves and main feedwater. Unit 2 is not affected," the licensee said.
The plant was stabilized in Mode 3, known as Hot Standby. Decay heat is being removed by discharging steam to the main condenser using the turbine bypass valves and main feedwater.
Unit 2 at the Saint Lucie facility was not affected.
According to NextEra Energy, Unit 1 at St. Lucie is back online at 100% power after operators safely resolved an equipment issue.
This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

About the role
Tasklet is building the AI platform companies use to run their business on agents. A customer describes an outcome in plain English, and Tasklet gets the work done across their tools and systems—immediately or in the cloud 24×7. We are building for real-world businesses, where making powerful agents simple, trustworthy, and easy to control matters just as much as making them intelligent.
This creates a defining product-design challenge: inventing how people and teams work with AI that does real work, not merely chats. We're looking for a Head of Design Engineering to own that experience holistically—making the entire product simple, intuitive, and beautiful, then personally implementing most of it in production.
This is an IC role, not a design-management role. You will work directly with our founders, customers, and engineers to decide how Tasklet should work, design it, and ship it. You will set the design bar for the company through your judgment, feedback, and example—not through process or a large team.
We need someone who has built something real and meaningful from scratch, ideally as a founder. You should be an exceptional product thinker, designer, and frontend engineer. This is one of the highest-leverage roles at Tasklet, and we're willing to pay accordingly.
Compensation
Salary
$300k → $450k
Equity
0.35% → 0.70%
Competitive benefits (medical, dental, vision, 401k, 4 weeks PTO, free lunch, etc.)
Responsibilities
Own Tasklet's product design end to end.
Make the whole product feel simple, intuitive, coherent, and beautiful—not just individual screens or features.
Build what you design.
You will personally write production code and ship most of your work. There is no traditional design-to-engineering handoff.
Invent the interaction model for AI work.
Make powerful agents understandable and trustworthy across latency, uncertainty, permissions, errors, human handoffs, and recovery. There is no playbook; you'll write it.
Simplify relentlessly.
Understand complex systems deeply enough to remove concepts, steps, and UI. Push back when the product is becoming harder to understand.
Obsess over the details.
Interaction, hierarchy, copy, motion, responsiveness, performance, accessibility, and reliability are all part of the design. Take Tasklet from good to a product people rave about.
Prototype and iterate at AI speed.
Use AI heavily across product exploration, design, implementation, and testing. Nearly every line of code at Tasklet is written with AI, and we expect you to use it as a serious creative and engineering collaborator.
Raise the design bar across the company.
Give direct, high-quality feedback; establish durable product principles and reusable patterns; and inspire everyone—not only designers—to make better product decisions.
Our ideal candidate
You're a hands-on engineer with exceptional design judgment.
You are fluent in modern frontend development and can take an idea all the way to polished production software yourself.
You've created something real from zero.
Ideally, you've been a founder or had equivalent ownership of a meaningful product from its earliest conception through real customer use. Your portfolio shows personal authorship, not just participation.
You think in products and systems, not screens.
You can form a clear mental model of a complicated system and turn it into something ordinary people immediately understand.
You have exceptional taste and sweat the details.
You care about the final 10% that separates functional software from software people love.
You lead while remaining an IC.

data.title: Tell HN: Cloudflare silently injects its analytics when you switch nameservers
data.author: stagas
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Cloudflare 是否会在代理网站中自动注入 JavaScript，以及这一行为的默认设置、透明度和安全影响。

不同观点：
• **功能解释派**：Cloudflare 在启用 Web Analytics、Email Address Obfuscation 等功能时，会向 HTML 注入统计或邮箱解码脚本；有人认为这是代理模式下提供流量与 DDoS 数据的必要手段。  
• **配置区分派**：若仅使用 Cloudflare DNS、域名设置为“DNS only”，HTTPS 直接连接源站，Cloudflare 通常无法修改 HTML；只有由 Cloudflare 终止 HTTPS 并反向代理时，才具备注入条件。  
• **反对与隐私安全担忧**：评论者认为，向原本纯 HTML、无 JavaScript 的网站强行添加 Cloudflare 脚本，类似旧式免费主机插广告，可能破坏网站设计与用户信任；有人称其为“hostile code”，并质疑是否涉及未经授权访问及美国《计算机欺诈与滥用法》。  
• **防护建议派**：建议使用 CSP 限制脚本来源，例如仅允许本站或指定域名；脚本示例还带有 SRI 完整性校验，但这并未消除对默认注入的疑虑。  
• **默认设置质疑派**：有人要求明确的退出机制，认为 Cloudflare 多次改变默认配置；另有用户发现新域名可能默认启用相关功能，导致“纯 JS-free”网站被注入脚本。

补充讨论：评论之间的争议焦点是“用户是否明确授权”以及 Cloudflare 的默认启用是否足够透明。部分用户分享了实际案例，也有人回忆旧式主机通过 HTML 标签、大小写或内容类型规避脚本注入的方法。

data.title: A SAT Attack on Tarski's High School Algebra Problem
data.author: matt_d
data.article_summary: 本文研究塔斯基“高中代数问题”：寻找满足其11条公理、却不满足威尔基恒等式的最小反模型。作者利用SAT证明，反模型最小规模为12（此前仅获猜想），并确定12元上共有8,957,952个同构类反模型，给出简洁分类。其方法优于Mace4、SEM等工具，并在Lean中形式化验证了主要结论。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕一项利用 SAT 求解器、对称性破缺和辅助变量技术研究代数恒等式/反例的工作，评论集中讨论其创新性、数学问题的范围、形式化验证的可信度及问题设定。

不同观点：
• 肯定 SAT 技术：zero_k 称赞 Markus Anders 的 Satsuma 对称性破缺系统及其竞赛成绩，并认为它明显快于 CryptoMiniSat 使用的 BreakID。NooneAtAll3 认为辅助变量可拆分内部子表达式、减少索引和约束规模。
• 质疑研究目标：NooneAtAll3 指出工作似乎不是解决整个 Tarski 问题，而是在寻找一个特定恒等式，并希望看到更多违背既有预期（如 Wilkie 结果）的算术模型。
• 质疑问题设定：munchler 认为代数中排除减法不自然，因为高中数学已熟悉减法；正是这一遗漏导致反例，因此结论的“揭示”令人失望。
• 质疑理论解释：dooglius 询问该问题是否已由哥德尔不完备定理说明不可能；406380581 则补充指出下界早已有先前工作建立。
• 质疑验证方式：LPisGood 认为依赖 ChatGPT/Codex 生成逾万行 Lean 代码并声称与 Python 输出“逐字节一致”说服力不足，人工审查成本和潜在错误令人担忧。

补充讨论：Abh1Works 将 SAT 误解为高中入学考试，属于术语歧义；争议核心是研究设定是否足够自然、结果是否真正新颖，以及 AI 辅助形式化能否达到可信的数学验证标准。

Title:
A SAT Attack on Tarski's High School Algebra Problem
Authors:
Bernardo Subercaseaux

Benjamin Przybocki
View a PDF of the paper titled A SAT Attack on Tarski's High School Algebra Problem, by Bernardo Subercaseaux and Benjamin Przybocki
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Tarski's high school algebra problem asks whether every true identity concerning addition, multiplication, and exponentiation of positive integers follows from a list of 11 elementary identities. Surprisingly, Wilkie showed that the following identity is valid over the positive integers and yet does not follow from Tarski's axioms: \begin{align*} &\left((1+x)^y + (1+x+x^2)^y\right)^x \cdot \left((1+x^3)^x + (1+x^2+x^4)^x\right)^y = \\ &\left((1+x)^x + (1+x+x^2)^x\right)^y \cdot \left((1+x^3)^y + (1+x^2+x^4)^y\right)^x. \end{align*} Gurevič gave an algebra on 59 elements that satisfies Tarski's axioms but not Wilkie's identity, and over the years several authors whittled down the size of such a countermodel, culminating in a countermodel of size 12 due to Burris and Yeats. On the other hand, Zhang proved that there is no countermodel with fewer than 11 elements. Using SAT, we prove that the smallest countermodels are of size 12, as conjectured by Burris and Yeats. Moreover, we show that there are exactly 8,957,952 countermodels on 12 elements up to isomorphism and provide a simple classification of them. Our SAT approach outperforms dedicated tools for finding countermodels in equational theories, namely Mace4 and SEM. Furthermore, using autoformalization, we prove the correctness of our main result in Lean.

data.article_summary: 文章介绍美国缅因州林业部门1918—1923年制作的森林火灾全景地图，均由土木工程师阿奇·诺克罗斯绘制。地图以瞭望塔为中心，标注地标，配合观测仪定位烟雾、协调灭火。文章还讲述作家凯鲁亚克1956年担任火警瞭望员的经历，以及瞭望塔后来被现代通信、卫星和摄像技术取代的变迁。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：通过《Firewatch》体验瞭望塔生活，及数字化体验是否会替代真实自然体验。

不同观点：
• 推荐观点：pimlottc认为，如果喜欢在森林瞭望塔度过夏天，《Firewatch》是一款值得推荐的独立叙事游戏，能够以游戏形式提供相关体验。  
• 质疑观点：bix6担心越来越多人被“从自然中带走”，转而通过电脑观看自然。虽然这种方式更高效，但可能损失真实置身自然的重要体验。  
• 审美与价值观点：bix6特别肯定游戏中的地图很美，同时暗示数字作品虽有视觉吸引力，却未必能替代自然本身。

补充讨论：争议焦点不在于游戏是否制作精美，而在于数字媒介带来的便利和效率，是否会以牺牲人与自然的直接联系为代价。

Archie G. Norcross’ Maine Forest Fire Maps (1918–22)
View from Double Top Forest Fire Station, Maine, 1919 —
Source
.
In the summer of 1956, the Beat writer Jack Kerouac ascended the North Cascade Mountains, climbing up through the glacial crests of Washington State to Desolation Peak, where he would assume a summer post as a fire lookout for the United States Forest Service. Alone in his sparsely furnished cabin in the sky, Kerouac kept watch for smoke, the first sign of forest fires. He was broke (
On The Road
was still a year away), and room, board, and $230 per month was a draw. But it was really on his friend Gary Snyder’s urging, the writer and Buddhist practitioner dubbed “Japhy” below, that the city slicker signed on. Kerouac was chasing an ascetic, meditative experience that would never really materialize. He would recall his sixty-three days of isolation in the semi-autobiographical
Desolation Angels
(1965), drawn from the journals he kept at the time, and
Dharma Bums
(1958):
Lo, in the morning I woke up and it was beautiful blue sunshine sky and I went out in my alpine yard and there it was, everything Japhy said it was, hundreds of miles of pure snow-covered rocks and virgin lakes and high timber, and below, instead of the world, I saw a sea of marshmallow clouds flat as a roof and extending miles and miles in every direction, creaming all the valleys, what they call low-level clouds, on my 6600-foot pinnacle it was all far below me. . . . I made bacon and eggs, dug a garbage pit a hundred yards down the trail, hauled wood and identified landmarks with my panoramic and firefinder and named all the magic rocks and clefts, names Japhy had sung to me so often. . .
The images featured here are versions of what Kerouac calls his “panoramic”: circular maps custom-made for the fire towers that once dotted the American wilderness like land-bound lighthouses. They come from the Maine Forestry Department, which erected dozens of steel towers — supporting lookouts some 12 to 48 feet (3.7 to 14.6 meters) above the craggy summits of the American Northeast — after a spate of devastating fires in 1903 and 1908. Like all of the panoramic maps produced for the Maine Fire District between 1918 and 1923, they were drawn by the civil engineer Archie G. Norcross (1880–1947).
Scroll through the whole page to download all images before printing.
View from Double Top Forest Fire Station (detail), Maine, 1919 —
Source
.
Each map takes a particular fire tower for its epicenter, orienting the lookout to his or her elevated universe: a world whose limits, more or less, are as far as the eye can see. Dotted with landmarks, panoramic maps made it possible to pinpoint a wildfire’s plume and coordinate teams of firefighters to extinguish it. They would have been accompanied by an alidade (Kerouac’s “firefinder”), a simple sighting device.
Gaining popularity in the early 1900s, the use of fire towers peaked in the mid-century, when improved communication technology, surveillance strategies, and “controlled burn” management began to take hold. Today, most of the 8000 lookouts have fallen into disrepair, superseded by camera networks, thermal satellite imaging, and aircraft patrols. A scant few remain active. Some are kept open as bare-bones shelters for passing hikers, who report wooden furniture and tin dishes left behind from over a century of use. The Doubletop Mountain lookout, for one, was dismantled sometime before 1972: according to the Forest Fire Lookout Association, it was “notorious for getting struck by lightning”.
Below you will find a selection of Norcross’ maps, courtesy of the Maine State Library via the DigitalMaine Repository. We've featured all the ones they've labeled with an open reuse license (in this case Creative Commons Attribution), but you can see a wider selection at
this link

data.title: The weekend is 100 years old
data.author: lentil_soup
data.article_summary: 文章回顾周末诞生一百周年。1926年，福特为工人实行每周五天、周末双休，周末由此成为劳动者共享的休息与社交时光。苏联取消固定周末的实验因造成家庭分离、士气低落而失败。如今，居家办公、周五“摸鱼”、周日处理工作及四天工作制使周末边界日益模糊，但其象征的自主、休息与集体生活仍具重要意义。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：七天制与周末并非天然存在，而是由宗教、工业化和社会制度逐步塑造；讨论延伸至工业时间制度对生活的影响及替代方案。

不同观点：
• **七天周是社会建构**：七天周没有天文依据，不同于日、月、季、年。早期美国因削弱欧洲节庆日、受清教徒传统影响，以每周安息日作为主要时间锚点；工业化、城市化、学校制度和按周发薪进一步固化“星期意识”。  
• **七天制曾是较“松”的界限**：前工业农业社会即使礼拜日也要照料牲畜；天主教社会节庆日较多，周界限不如清教徒社会明确。机械化工厂出现后，时间才更容易被标准化、机械化管理。  
• **周末是近代产物**：有人指出“一天周末”古老，而“两天周末”仅约一百年；许多看似历史悠久的西方规范，其实是近150年的英语世界尤其美国创造。  
• **工业时钟与个人自主的张力**：有人追问如何不受工业时钟支配，认为稳定工作、家庭责任和社会交往使个人难以脱离固定时间制度；也有人质疑“夺回自主权”是否只是短期休息的夸张表述。  
• **支持缩短工时**：评论者关注休息日的具体时间，因为休假若无法与家人同步意义有限，因而支持四天工作制并期待其普及；也有“每周五都过劳动节”等幽默倡议。  
• **制度重构与玩笑方案**：有人提出五天一周、跨周末安排及重新设计月份的历法，体现对现行时间制度的实验性反思。

补充讨论：评论还强调近两百年生活变化极其剧烈，并推荐相关劳动史著作；争议焦点在于缩短工作周能否真正实现生活自主，以及社会是否具备转型条件。

The introduction of the weekend gave rise to the minibreak – alongside plenty of other leisure activities.
Composite: getty images/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
The introduction of the weekend gave rise to the minibreak – alongside plenty of other leisure activities.
Composite: getty images/Getty Images
Work-life balance
The weekend is 100 years old – but have ‘skiveday Fridays’ and hybrid working ruined it for everyone?
In 1926, Henry Ford gave his employees both Saturdays and Sundays off – and the two-day chunk of time to party, pray or simply do nothing was born. Now it’s changed beyond recognition
Jess Cartner-Morley
Sun 16 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT
Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 03.20 EDT
Share
Prefer the Guardian on Google
F
or 11 years, from 1929 to 1940, the Soviet Union did not have weekends. Instead, to increase productivity citizens were allocated a day off in every seven at random. With 80% of the population at work on any given day, factories never had to power down.
A letter from a disgruntled worker to Pravda newspaper, published soon after the implementation of this new working calendar, outlined the problems: “What is there for us to do at home if our wives are in the factory, our children at school, and nobody can visit us?” the letter-writer asked. “It is no holiday if you have to have it alone.” Parents found themselves at home while their children were at school, or with kids unsupervised while they were on shift. With no shared day off, extended family gatherings became impossible. The workforce became demoralised and listless, the projected spike in productivity never materialised, and the policy was first modified, then abandoned altogether.
Eleven years, though. Is that not absolutely wild? A world without weekends feels impossible. A world without Saturday Night Fever, without Manic Monday. We may no longer go to church on Sunday, but we still worship the weekend. “The weekend looms large because it represents the triumph of collective time over market time,” says Brad Beaven, professor of social and cultural history at the University of Portsmouth. “It is not just about rest, but about reclaiming autonomy from the industrial clock.”
View image in fullscreen
‘We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – like the distant roar of a lawnmower.’
Photograph: Cavan Images/Liz DeGroff/Getty Images/Cavan Images RF
Saturday and Sunday, sacred to the dignity and humanity of working people, are laden with mythology and ceremony. From Cilla Black to Gary Lineker, the main characters of our weekends become giants of the culture. We romanticise the weekend, even the prosaic bits – the distant roar of a lawnmower, the rattle of classified football results on the radio. Everyone knows what a weekend means. The snap of a laptop cover at 4.58pm on a Friday. The clink of the first pint glass and the smell of chips on the way home. The slow-motion pace of a weekend pavement, the gear change from hustle to meander. The rituals have changed with the times, of course, and people-watching at brunch on Saturday is now as much of a tradition as cooking a roast at home on Sunday. A weekend changes shape as you move through life stages, but in each iteration it remains a shared experience between you and your peers.
“The weekend that I had when I was 20 was very different from the weekend that I have now, at 40 and with kids,” laughs Pedro Gomes, professor of economics at Birkbeck, University of London and author of the book Friday is the New Saturday. “When you are young, you are bonding with your friends, and then when you get older, you might be with your family. Eventually, you might be with grandchildren. We move through different manifestations of the weekend, in our lifetimes.”
But it can be hard to pin down, these days, where a weekend begins and ends. Laundry gets done on a work-from-home Friday, but emails are answered on Sunday. A shopping splurge is as likely to be a cheer-up treat on your phone after a tough Wednesday as a Saturday outing. The traditional Saturday 3pm football kick-off has been stretched across the television schedules all the way to Monday evening. The four-day week – first predicted by Richard Nixon, of all people, in 1956 – has become a reality in the Netherlands, with people working an average of 32.1 hours. Friday is forging ahead with a quiet secession from the working week without anyone signing off the paperwork. It raises the question: what even is “the weekend” in 2026?
R
emarkably, the concept of the weekend as we know it is only 100 years old. In 1926, Henry Ford changed the shape of the week, announcing that the workers at his factories would now do five eight-hour days instead of six, with no cut in pay. Ford did not invent the weekend – the idea had been bubbling under for a century, in campaigns by trade unions, religious groups and progressive employers – but by putting his considerable industrial weight behind it, the two-day chunk of freedom was born.

data.title: Does anyone run Postgres without PgBouncer?
data.author: abelanger
data.article_summary: 文章探讨托管型Postgres是否普遍使用连接池。由于Postgres不擅长管理大量连接，生产环境通常需要本地连接池和PgBouncer。作者调查发现，几乎所有主流云服务商都内置PgBouncer或类似方案，说明连接池已属核心能力。但各家配置方式和限制不一，增加了用户与供应商的重复成本。作者主张将连接池原生整合进Postgres，提供统一数据库地址和端口，减少运维复杂度。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：是否应使用 PgBouncer，以及应用层连接池与外部连接池的适用边界。

不同观点：
• **无需默认使用**：传统应用、非 Serverless、实例较少且可由应用/ORM管理连接池时，直连 PostgreSQL 更简单；Python 多进程或连接 churn 较高时才更需要 PgBouncer。Go 的 pgx、Node 等内置池已能满足不少场景。  
• **规模化后应使用**：PostgreSQL 每连接一个进程，连接风暴或数百连接会明显损害性能；PgBouncer 可减少到达数据库的连接数，避免未来扩容时“措手不及”。  
• **两类池机制不同**：应用池多采用 FIFO，追求低延迟但会长期维持大量“热连接”；PgBouncer 倾向 LIFO，使多余连接冷却并关闭，更注重数据库吞吐。  
• **PgBouncer有代价**：会增加部署和运维复杂度，激进池化还可能影响预编译语句等功能；小流量应用、CI/CD或仅服务单一应用的数据库，使用它可能是过度设计。  
• **应内置于Postgres**：既然连接池几乎是常见需求，部分评论认为核心应原生支持，而非依赖独立组件。PgBouncer 已较成熟、可配置，且预编译语句支持改善后更适合默认使用。

补充讨论：Neon 认为 PgBouncer 在多租户和高可用部署上有限，正探索替代方案；RDS Proxy 因价格较高未必普及。争议焦点是“提前为扩展付复杂度”还是“避免连接激增风险”。

Does anyone run Postgres without PgBouncer?
Published
AugÂ 12,Â 2026
I'm on X/Twitter at
@brandur
.
AugÂ 12,Â 2026
I got a nice shout-out from
Ben Dicken over the weekend
on an old article I’d written on
managing database connections
. (This guy is apparently the Mick Jagger of databases, because I can’t remember having gotten so many inbound LinkedIn invitations in one day before.)
Something that hit hard is that I wrote this article almost
ten years ago
.
Just as striking is that as I was reading back through it, I realized that despite being a decade old, it’s still pretty much up to date. Postgres is still, shall we say, not
great
at managing lots of connections, so you want to use local connection pools, short-term checkouts, and a pooler like PgBouncer.
It got me wondering:
how
standard is it to use a pooler, exactly? To answer that question, I made a table of all managed Postgres providers with household notoriety and whether they support PgBouncer, something close to PgBouncer, or no connection pooling at all.

Not only is PgBouncer support widespread, but we see above that the overwhelming majority of providers bundle it out of the box. I’d go a step further – since neither IBM nor Oracle is a service that any self-respecting person not part of an enterprise sales cycle would actually use,
one hundred percent
of plausible managed Postgres providers bundle a pooler.
If everyone needs it, is it really a non-core function?
In some ways, it could be argued that this status quo is okay. Users that need a connection pooler have access to one, and can use it to keep prod stable.
But there’s undoubtedly a lot of wasted effort here. Every provider has had to come up with their own homegrown mechanism for getting multiple components set up and configured and establish a convention for where to find Postgres versus its bouncer. Every user needs to
reference a guide
explaining PgBouncer’s limitations (e.g. don’t listen/notify) and read about its
pooling modes and tradeoffs
.
Imagine if you went to your local car dealership and they sold you a car without a windshield. On the way over you’d noticed that 100% of vehicles on the road did in fact have windshields, and for good reason because it turns out to be pretty dangerous to drive without one. Since you were the one that bought the car, it’d be hard to argue that it’s not your responsibility now to outfit it with a windshield before it’s roadworthy, but it’d
also
be fair to later be pissed off at the dealer for selling a vehicle that can’t just be driven off the lot.
Reintegration
What if there was a world where you went to your favorite Postgres provider and you got one database URL, one port, and no extra configuration or caveats to worry about? Your managed provider doesn’t need to add an aftermarket windshield because one came with the car already. We know a place like this can exist because that’s already how things work in MySQL and Mongo-land.
There are reasons it doesn’t happen, like reviving the age-old processes versus threads debate, which very few contributors are venerated enough to push for progress on, but given the developer-years’ worth of effort in working around Postgres’ lack of connection pooling, it’s hard to argue this wouldn’t be one of the highest-impact operational improvements possible.

.
49277952.article_summary: 文章探讨托管型Postgres是否普遍使用连接池。由于Postgres不擅长管理大量连接，生产环境通常需要本地连接池和PgBouncer。作者调查发现，几乎所有主流云服务商都内置PgBouncer或类似方案，说明连接池已属核心能力。但各家配置方式和限制不一，增加了用户与供应商的重复成本。作者主张将连接池原生整合进Postgres，提供统一数据库地址和端口，减少运维复杂度。
49277952.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：是否应使用 PgBouncer，以及应用层连接池与外部连接池的适用边界。

不同观点：
• **无需默认使用**：传统应用、非 Serverless、实例较少且可由应用/ORM管理连接池时，直连 PostgreSQL 更简单；Python 多进程或连接 churn 较高时才更需要 PgBouncer。Go 的 pgx、Node 等内置池已能满足不少场景。  
• **规模化后应使用**：PostgreSQL 每连接一个进程，连接风暴或数百连接会明显损害性能；PgBouncer 可减少到达数据库的连接数，避免未来扩容时“措手不及”。  
• **两类池机制不同**：应用池多采用 FIFO，追求低延迟但会长期维持大量“热连接”；PgBouncer 倾向 LIFO，使多余连接冷却并关闭，更注重数据库吞吐。  
• **PgBouncer有代价**：会增加部署和运维复杂度，激进池化还可能影响预编译语句等功能；小流量应用、CI/CD或仅服务单一应用的数据库，使用它可能是过度设计。  
• **应内置于Postgres**：既然连接池几乎是常见需求，部分评论认为核心应原生支持，而非依赖独立组件。PgBouncer 已较成熟、可配置，且预编译语句支持改善后更适合默认使用。

补充讨论：Neon 认为 PgBouncer 在多租户和高可用部署上有限，正探索替代方案；RDS Proxy 因价格较高未必普及。争议焦点是“提前为扩展付复杂度”还是“避免连接激增风险”。

data.title: Stop Turning every purchase into a tip request
data.author: gist
data.article_summary: 文章批评美国电子支付小费泛滥：咖啡店、外卖、零售等场景常以高比例选项和“无小费”按钮隐藏制造心理压力，使小费从对优质服务的奖励变成交易附加费。作者认为商家应直接公开真实价格，保障消费者自愿给小费，也维护顾客、员工和企业之间的信任。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕美国“预设小费”与小费文化的合理性、责任归属及其对消费者和服务业员工的影响展开讨论。

不同观点：
• **反对非必要场景小费**：有人认为理发、按摩等直接接触身体或提供个性化服务应给小费；取餐、柜台结账、自助服务只是收银或交付商品，不应被要求小费，可直接选择“免小费”。  
• **主张抵制强制提示小费的商家**：仅选择零小费不足以改变现状，应停止光顾在结账时加入小费界面的外带、柜台服务店；但也有人指出，抵制最终可能伤害依赖小费谋生的员工。  
• **将责任归于支付系统和商业模式**：支付处理商预设18%/20%/25%等选项，并从小费中抽成约1%，推动了小费扩张；商家则可借小费抵扣工资、压低菜单价格，把劳动力成本转嫁给顾客。  
• **批评“道德绑架”**：顾客即使经济拮据，也会因不小费而感到羞愧，被暗示为“剥削员工”或“不该消费”；小费反而加重了无力支付者的负担。  
• **质疑预付小费的合理性**：商品或服务尚未完成、质量未知，消费者不明白为何要先付小费，也担心服务不好却无法追回。  
• **更激进立场**：有人提出“永不小费”运动，认为美国缺乏完善员工权利，小费文化实际上掩盖了低工资和劳动保障不足的问题。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于小费究竟是对优质服务的自愿奖励，还是商家逃避正常工资责任、利用支付界面和社会压力转嫁成本的机制。另有评论批评相关文章疑似由AI生成，属于对内容质量的旁支质疑。

49323874.article_content:
close
Video
Tip screen guilt trips have turned American generosity into a surcharge
President of Exit Stage Left Advisors Ted Jenkin joins Fox News Digital to breakdown the increase in tipping costs and surge of tipping screens in restaurants and businesses.
NEW
You can now listen to Fox News articles!
I have no problem tipping. I love tipping for a job well done. It’s part of American culture.
However, I do have a problem being manipulated into it.
America didn't just create a tipping culture. We’ve created a
guilt culture
coupled with technology. Somewhere between the pandemic and the explosion of digital payment screens, saying "thank you" quietly became a financial obligation. What used to be a reward for exceptional service has turned into an expectation for simply completing a transaction.
Is there anything more annoying than a takeout employee saying, "The computer just wants to ask you a question?" Guess what, it didn’t ask me how happy I was with the service but instead asked how much I wanted to leave for a tip.
A person selects a custom tip amount at Miller's Ale House in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla.
(Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group)
Today, whether you're buying a latte, picking up takeout, ordering frozen yogurt or grabbing a sandwich, you're often confronted with the same three oversized buttons: 20%. 25%. 30%. In one place, I saw four buttons of 18%, 20%, 22% and 25%.
Notice what's missing?
Fifteen percent.
Apparently, gratitude now starts at 18% where generosity used to end.
Video
Let's be clear. This isn't about hardworking servers, bartenders or delivery drivers. Many depend on tips, and they deserve to be rewarded for outstanding service.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS ARE CHANGING DINING AS CUSTOMERS EAT HALF THEIR MEALS, TAKE REST HOME, CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS
This is about
businesses
discovering that it's easier to ask customers to absorb higher labor costs than to honestly raise their prices. And it’s easier to make it difficult for people to instantaneously opt out rather than quickly opt in.
Instead of charging what something actually costs, they've outsourced the uncomfortable conversation to an iPad.
The menu says one thing. The checkout screen says another. That's not transparency. That's behavioral marketing.
Even worse, tipping has escaped the restaurant and invaded nearly every corner of American life. Coffee shops. Bakeries. Stadium concession stands. Airport kiosks. Food trucks. Self-serve frozen yogurt. Retail counters. Even places where the only interaction is someone handing you the item you already paid for, like the six bagels I picked out and picked up the other day.
Is there anything more annoying than a takeout employee saying, "The computer just wants to ask you a question?"
We're no longer tipping for service. We're tipping for existence.
STARBUCKS USES CHATGPT TO SUGGEST DRINKS BASED ON MOOD AS EXPERT WARNS OF HIDDEN DOWNSIDES
And let's stop pretending those payment screens are neutral. They aren't. They're designed to make you hesitate before pressing "No Tip." If you can find the "No Tip" button to begin with on the screen. The employee is watching. It’s uncomfortable. The next customer is waiting. Nobody wants to feel like the villain over a cup of coffee.
Businesses understand human psychology. That's why those screens don't ask, "Would you like to leave a tip?"
They ask, "How generous are you?"
There's another consequence no one talks about. As expected, tips keep climbing, but
consumers
don't become more generous. They become more skeptical. They start tipping less enthusiastically, dining out less frequently, or avoiding businesses that constantly make them feel like they're being shaken down on a street corner.
GROCERY BOSS WARNS MAMDANI'S CITY-RUN STORES PIT GOVERNMENT AGAINST 'ITS OWN CITIZENS'
That's bad for customers. It's bad for workers. And it's bad for the businesses that started the trend.
Video
Here's a radical idea.
If your hamburger costs $24 to sell profitably, charge $24. If your coffee needs to cost $6, put $6 on the menu. Stop advertising one price while hoping social pressure collects another 25% at checkout.
Americans have always been generous. We donate billions to
charity
. We help neighbors after hurricanes. We rally around families facing hardship. We reward people who go above and beyond.
But generosity only has value when it's freely given.
The moment it becomes expected, preprogrammed and accompanied by a digital guilt trip, it stops feeling like gratitude and starts feeling like a surcharge.
A tip was never supposed to be another tax.
Let's be clear. This isn't about hardworking servers, bartenders or delivery drivers. Many depend on tips, and they deserve to be rewarded for outstanding service.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION
It was supposed to be a thank-you.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Maybe it's time America remembered the difference.
CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TED JENKIN
Ted Jenkin is President of
Exit Stage Left Ad
